newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK rate rise will not stall property boom -Salomon.
newsitem.headline: HK rate rise will not stall property boom -Salomon.

text.p: Hong Kong's booming land and property markets might be tempered by a rise in short-term interest rates, but the underlying trend remains up, Salomon Brothers analyst Michael Green said on Wednesday.

Speaking the morning after a fiercely fought auction led to a record HK$11.82 billion (US$1.53 billion) being paid for a waterfront site likely to allow a floor area of 2.18 million square feet, Green said he would welcome a Hong Kong rate hike following an overnight quarter point U.S. rate rise.
"U.S. interest rates having gone up by 25 basis points is certainly positive for the (property) market at this point," Green said.
"We are now in a situation where we have had rampant speculation and a rise in rates can take the 'flare' off the market -- and reduce the propensity for government intervention," Green added.
Stock market sources have speculated that a meeting between the government and the Property Developers Association could lead to measures to try to cool the sector.
Later in the day, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority did raise its own discount rate, the Liquidity Adjustment Rate, by 25 basis points in reaction to the Fed move.
Local Hong Kong banks followed suit by increasing their prime lending rates by the same margin to 8.75 percent.
Green, a leading expert on Hong Kong's property market, said Salomon believed the cyclical trend remained upwards.

"Our forecast for price increases in 1997 is for 10 percent, and we've already seen 6.0 percent of that. During 1998 our forecast is for 15 percent, and for 1999 up to 20 percent -- though it could be a lot lower," he said.

He said the indications were clear that developers, like many other businessmen, have complete confidence in Hong Kong for several years beyond the handover of the territory to China scheduled for June 30 this year.
"I think the handover now is just a formality," he said.

Hong Kong's desperate need for residential property, where the rate of building new homes is currently only satisfying net immigration, would keep underpinning price growth, especially in the absence of a comprehensive, medium-term government plan to free up supply and ease mortgage regulations, Green said.
Yet uncertainties over immigration patterns from China in the next few years and the potential for knock-ons from further U.S. rate moves would also stimulate volatility, he added.
